title: When the Gods Did the Work
sum: The poem opens in a time before humans, when gods had to do the work. The great Anunnaki made the junior gods, the Igigi, carry the basket of earth. The three highest gods drew lots for the world: Anu took heaven, Enlil the earth, and Enki the fresh waters below, with the bolt that keeps the sea in place.

Then the Igigi dug the rivers and canals, the Tigris and the Euphrates, raised the mountains and made the marshes. The middle of the passage is badly broken. It ends with the gods carrying the load for years upon years, by night and by day.
readings: Read as a story about work

The first line sets the theme of the whole poem: who has to work, and why. The gods are "man" because they do a man's labor. Everything that follows, the strike, the making of humans and the Flood, grows from this load.

Genesis also begins with a divided world (sky, sea and land), rivers that water the land, and a question of work. But in Genesis one God makes everything by his word, owns all of it, works without tiring and rests because the work is finished (Genesis 1; Genesis 2:2-3).

views.C: A Christian reader sees an honest question, why life is so much hard work, answered with gods who are as worn out as their worshipers. The Bible's God divides nothing by lot: "To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it" (Psalm 24:1), and he "never tires" (Isaiah 40:28).
views.H: Assyriologists read the opening as a picture of the Babylonian state set in heaven: a king, officials, and a labor gang digging canals. The first line's grammar is debated (Lambert and Millard, von Soden, the SEAL editors). Millard noted that the poem is the only Babylonian work that, like Genesis, runs in one story from the making of humans to the Flood.
views.M: For its first hearers the gods ranked like a royal court: Anu the distant father, Enlil the active ruler of the earth from his temple at Nippur, Enki the wise lord of the fresh waters. Canals were the life of the land, and digging them was the heaviest duty a king could lay on his people.
views.S: Christian readers who see real spiritual powers behind the nations' gods read the sharing out of the world beside Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where the Most High divides the nations and keeps Jacob for himself (see the topic divine-council). Others read the scene as human imagination only, since "every god of the peoples is a nothing-god" (Psalm 96:5).
views.J: Homer's Iliad has the same picture of three brothers casting lots for sky, sea and underworld (Iliad 15.187-193). Jewish and Christian writers never adopted it: the Bible's God gives the earth to human beings (Psalm 115:16).

deep.h: What the opening tells us about the whole poem
deep.b:
The first line, inūma ilū awīlum, became the poem's name. However it is read (see the note on 1:1), it puts gods and humans in the same sentence and makes work the link between them. The gods "bore the work, they carried the work basket" (1:2). Later the same basket is laid on humans (3:10; 3:74). A. R. Millard summed up the poem's idea: man was made "to free the gods from the toil of ordering the earth to produce their food."

Genesis starts somewhere else entirely: with God speaking a good world into being (Genesis 1:31), and humans made in his image to rule it (Genesis 1:26-28). Work is there too (Genesis 2:15), but it is a calling before it becomes a burden (Genesis 3:17-19).

deep.title: A world that belongs to no one god
deep.b: My reading: the lots of 1:11-1:16 explain much of what follows. Because the world is split among Anu, Enlil and Enki, no one god is in charge of everything. Enlil rules the earth but needs Anu's backing and Enki's skill; Enki can work around Enlil's decisions. The Flood story later turns on exactly this split: one god decrees destruction and another quietly saves a man. In the Bible, the one who judges and the one who saves are the same God (Genesis 6:13; Genesis 6:18).

echoes: Genesis 2:2-3; Genesis 2:10-15; Psalm 24:1; Psalm 115:16; Job 38:8-11; Deuteronomy 32:8-9; Psalm 81:6

settings.to: those who heard or read the poem
settings.why: To set the scene: a world without humans, where the gods themselves had to dig and carry, so that the rest of the story can explain why humans exist and why they work.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils. The main copy was written at Sippar by Ipiq-Aya, who signs himself a junior scribe, in the reign of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (mid-1600s BC); later copies were made in Babylon, at Nineveh in Assyria and again at Sippar centuries later.

title: The Gods' Strike
sum: The worn-out Igigi grumble in the trench. Their spokesman, the god We-ila, urges them to depose Enlil. They burn their spades and baskets and, in the middle of the night, surround Enlil's temple, the Ekur.

Enlil's servants wake him. Pale with fear, he calls Anu and Enki, and the great gods hold a hearing. Nusku is sent out to ask who leads the revolt. The answer comes back: all of them, because the work is killing them. Enlil weeps, offers to go up to heaven with Anu, and asks that one god be singled out to bear the sentence.
readings: The scene is a strike told in the language of a Babylonian work camp: baskets, spades, overseers, a ringleader, a night march to the boss's house. The poem takes the strikers' side: even the great gods admit the work is too heavy (3:4).

Christian readers think of other rebellions among heavenly beings: the Watchers of 1 Enoch, Isaiah's "Shining One," the dragon's angels in Revelation 12. The contrast is the point: in the Bible rebellion against God is pride and sin, and God is never afraid.

views.C: The Christian reader notices how small these gods are: asleep, frightened, weeping, unable to rule without a vote. The God of Israel "does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4), hears the cry of forced laborers (Exodus 3:7) and frees them, instead of passing the load to someone else.
views.H: Scholars read the strike against the background of the corvée, the forced labor that Babylonian kings demanded for canals. The episode is long and repetitive in the old copy, and the later copies change details: who speaks (Enlil or Anu, 2:89), whether the rebels "rebelled" or "shouted" (2:120), and whether they mean to confront or kill the officer (2:5).
views.M: The hearers knew the setting: the Ekur, Enlil's temple at Nippur; Nusku, his minister; a council of great gods; night watches; officials with court titles. The gods' world copies the human state, and its crises are a king's crises.
views.S: Christian writers have long read the gods of the nations as fallen spiritual powers. Justin Martyr wrote that angels who sinned with women fathered the beings called demons, and that the poets gave their deeds to the gods (Second Apology 5). Augustine called the pagan gods spirits eager to do harm (City of God 8.22). Michael Heiser reads Psalm 82 as God judging divine beings who ruled the nations. Others read the scene only as myth, since the idols are "nothing" (1 Corinthians 8:4). Both readings stand on Scripture (1 Corinthians 10:20).
views.J: Helge Kvanvig compares the Igigi's revolt with the Watchers story of 1 Enoch 6-16: in Atrahasis the rebellion leads to humans made to toil; in 1 Enoch to giants for whom humans must toil. The Watchers' oath on Mount Hermon (1 Enoch 6:4-6) is a pact of heavenly beings against heaven's order, but their sin is lust and forbidden teaching, not overwork.

deep.h: Who's who: the Igigi and the Watchers
deep.b:
What fits: both are groups of heavenly beings who act together against the order set by higher powers; both stories lead, in the end, to the Flood (1 Enoch 10; Atrahasis Tablet III). Kvanvig has studied the two side by side.

What does not: the Igigi are junior gods doing manual labor; the Watchers are angels set to watch over the world. The Igigi strike over work and are vindicated: the gods admit their load was too heavy. The Watchers come down to take human wives and teach forbidden arts, and are judged and bound (1 Enoch 10:4-12). The Igigi are never punished.

Verdict: unlikely to be the same beings or the same story. The shared shape, heavenly beings in revolt before the Flood, is real and worth noticing, but the reasons and the endings are opposite.

deep.title: The noise begins at Enlil's door
deep.b: My reading: the word rigmu, "noise," first appears when the striking gods surround the Ekur (2:41). After humans are made, Mami says the noise has been passed to them (3:76), and later Enlil tries to silence it with plague, drought and flood. Read this way, the poem's "noise" is the cry of overworked laborers, first gods, then humans. The Bible hears that cry differently: "Their plea for help rose up to God from their labor" (Exodus 2:23).

echoes: Exodus 1:13-14; Exodus 2:23; Exodus 3:7; Psalm 121:4; 1 Kings 18:27; 1 Kings 22:19-20; Psalm 82:1-7; Isaiah 14:12-14; Revelation 12:7-9; Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4; 1 Enoch 6:1-6; Daniel 3:8

title: Clay, Blood and Spittle
sum: Enki takes the strikers' side: their work really is too heavy. He proposes that the birth goddess Mami make a human being to carry the gods' basket. Mami answers that she needs Enki's help and his clay. Enki sets up a purifying bath on the first, seventh and fifteenth days of the month; one god, We-ila, "who had understanding," is slaughtered, and Nintu mixes his flesh and blood with clay. A ghost comes from the god's flesh, so that he will not be forgotten.

The Igigi spit on the clay. Mami announces that the work is done: the gods' load is laid on man, and their noise passes to humankind. The freed gods kiss her feet and call her Mistress of All the Gods. In the House of Destiny the birth goddesses tread the clay, Mami recites the spell, pinches off fourteen lumps, sets a brick between them and draws the reed knife, and seven males and seven females are shaped.
readings: Read as the making of a worker
The purpose is stated again and again: "let man carry the god's work basket" (3:10, 3:22). Humans are the solution to the gods' labor dispute. The poem is frank that this costs a god's life.
The second half of the chapter is a birth scene: midwives, a spell, a brick, a knife for the cord, males and females in pairs. The poem explains every human birth by the first one.

views.C: Genesis tells the same moment from the other side. God does not need a worker; he makes humankind "in our image" to rule (Genesis 1:26-28), shapes the man himself and breathes into him the breath of life (Genesis 2:7), and sets him in a garden to work and guard it (Genesis 2:15). No god dies to make humans; it is God the Son who later gives his own life, willingly, to set them free (Acts 20:28; Matthew 20:28).
views.H: Scholars stress how much of this is shared Mesopotamian tradition: humans made from clay and a slain god's blood (also Enuma Elish VI), a mother goddess, a council. Millard compared Genesis point by point; Gerhard Hasel argued that Genesis 1 deliberately answers this picture of human purpose. The copies differ in places, sometimes reversing the sense (3:25).
views.M: Every detail touched the hearers' religion: moon-day purification rites, the birth goddess and her helpers, the brick of birth, the spell spoken over a woman in labor, the ghost that the family remembers after death. The poem explains why humans serve the gods in temples: they were made to.
views.S: Some Christian readers see in the slain god and the spit-moistened clay a dark copy of truths the Bible tells rightly: humans made from earth with a divine gift in them, and a divine death that brings life. Others see only human guesses about origins. The site labels the strongest of these links as Claude's own theories (3:39; 3:50).
views.J: Irenaeus read Jesus' clay of spittle in John 9 as the hand of God that first shaped Adam (Against Heresies 5.15.2). Jewish and Christian writers kept the clay and the potter (Isaiah 64:8; Job 33:6) and left out the slain god entirely.

deep.h: Did Genesis borrow from this story?
deep.b:
Three main answers are given.

Borrowing and reworking. Many scholars hold that Israel took over Mesopotamian traditions and reshaped them. Millard quotes Gerhard von Rad's view that both flood stories are independent forms of a still older tradition, which Israel met in Canaan and absorbed into its faith, and names C. A. Simpson and S. H. Hooke as holding that Israel adopted and adapted Babylonian stories.

A deliberate answer. Gerhard Hasel argued that Genesis 1 "combats pagan mythological notions": humans are not an afterthought to feed the gods but the only creatures God blesses, and God gives them food.

A shared memory, truly kept in Genesis. A. R. Millard concluded that it "has yet to be shown that there was borrowing"; that the two traditions describe the same events, which Babylonians could only tell "in their own polytheistic language" while "the Hebrews, or their ancestors, understood the action of God in it"; and that the likenesses in the making of humans (clay and a divine part) may be ideas that arose in more than one place.

The site does not decide between the second and third answers, which many believing scholars combine. All three agree on what matters most here: the purpose of humankind differs at the root.

deep.title: Replacement workers, or images of God?
deep.b: My reading: the poem and Genesis 1 ask the same question, "what are humans for?", and their answers face each other almost line by line. In Atrahasis the council says "let man carry the god's work basket" (3:10); in Genesis God says "Let us make humankind in our image ... Let them rule" (Genesis 1:26). Here a god is butchered and his blood mixed in; there God breathes his own breath (Genesis 2:7). Here the gods are set free from work; there God rests, and then gives rest to his creatures (Genesis 2:2-3; Mark 2:27). Hasel and Millard made parts of this comparison; the line-by-line pairing is mine.
